definition: Acculturation is the gradual taking-on of another culture's customs and habits through long contact with it — new ways absorbed while much of one's own culture stays.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word acculturation. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know acculturation should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her first year abroad was one long acculturation: new greetings, new queue manners, new small talk — and her grandmother's Sunday recipes untouched.
Adjustment is milder than acculturation: an adjustment swaps a schedule or a phrase to get through the week, while acculturation reworks habits, manners, and speech through years of contact.
Assimilation goes further than acculturation — acculturation adds a second culture's ways alongside your own, while assimilation absorbs the original culture until little of it remains visible.

Immersion is the setting, not the change: you can be immersed in a culture — surrounded by it, schooled in it — for a season and come home unchanged. Acculturation is what long immersion can produce: the new ways actually take root in your habits and speech.

Integration is the civic, two-way word — a community and its newcomers adjusting institutions until both fit. Acculturation happens inside the newcomers themselves: it names the customs and manners one group's members absorb from another.

Acculturation is the gradual taking-on of another culture's customs and habits through long contact with it — new ways absorbed while much of one's own culture stays.
When the Duarte family moved from Lisbon to Winnipeg, acculturation crept in through the small things.
Within two winters the children were talking hockey at breakfast and packing maple cookies beside the custard tarts; Mr.
Duarte learned to shovel a neighbor's walk without being asked.
And still, every Christmas Eve, the table filled with salt cod, exactly as it had at home.
Acculturation is the exact word for that slow shift, because it names the process of absorbing a new culture's ways through steady contact — greetings, foods, and habits picked up year by year.
It is not erasure: the Duartes take on Canadian customs without surrendering their Portuguese ones.
When the old identity dissolves entirely, the word is assimilation.
Acculturation is the social scientist's word for culture rubbing off through contact, and it keeps both cultures in the frame — the new one arriving, the old one persisting.
When the original identity is swallowed outright, the word is assimilation; when a body rather than a culture adapts — to altitude, to heat — the word is acclimatization.
On the SAT it lives in history and social-science passages about migration and empire, always as a process of years, never a single event.

Marek stepped off the train in Chicago in 1912 with a toolbox, a prayer book, and no English beyond 'good morning.' The mills set the rhythm of his days, and slowly they set more than that.
Within a few years he was scoring baseball games on Sundays and arguing union politics in quick, confident English.
His letters home traced a gradual acculturation: new holidays kept alongside old ones, American idioms folded into Polish sentences.
Yet every December the carols in his kitchen were Polish, and his daughters learned them word for word.
He had not traded one country for another, his eldest wrote later; he had learned to carry both.
